Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette: Vikram was forty-one when the night finally broke. It had started like any other evening, but when his partner's voice rose, the room seemed to tilt. He remembered the exact moment the conversation fractured: a few disjointed phrases followed by overlapping syllables that refused to cohere into meaning. Then came the scent of whiskey spilling onto the counter, thick and sharp. A wave of nausea rolled through his stomach before his mind could name the danger. His body was already bracing, muscles locking, when the first blow landed. The months that followed were not a continuous film but a series of frozen frames-his partner's raised arm, the scarlet stain on his knuckles, the way the light caught glass shattering on the floor. Each image arrived in his mind with the same unmediated intensity as the original terror, as clear and unyielding as photographs left too long in the sun. In the weeks after he moved out, Vikram's nervous system refused to stand down. He learned to measure his days by the speed of his own reactions. A car backfiring on the commute to the firm would jolt his shoulders forward before he could identify the sound. He stopped leaving the office after six, telling himself he was catching up on renderings, but the truth was simpler: the city after dark felt like a threshold he had no right to cross. Sleep became a negotiation he consistently lost. He lay rigid beneath the covers, eyes fixed on the ceiling, convinced that dropping his guard would let the past slip back through the cracks. What frightened him most was not the noise itself, but the certainty that his body had already sounded an alarm his mind could not silence. By autumn, his work as an architect had become a map of narrow corridors. During a site walk at a downtown development, three contractors began arguing in rapid, overlapping tongues. Vikram felt the familiar sickening lurch in his gut, his hands instinctively curling around his tablet. He excused himself and walked to the break room, where the scent of a colleague's flask triggered a sharp, immediate wave of physical unwellness that left him gripping the counter until it passed. Over the following months, he began declining firm mixers, skipping client luncheons, and turning down weekend trips. He told his wife, Elena, he was overwhelmed with deadlines, but the distance between them widened. He could not bring himself to be near the very spaces that once felt like home. Vikram's silence at home grew heavier than any blueprint. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own judgment, that the man who once promised protection had failed in his most important role, a failure that felt especially heavy within a South Asian American family that had always valued steadfast partnership. Every time he hesitated before answering Elena's questions, he felt the weight of that betrayal pressing against his ribs. He was certain he had let someone who depended on him down, and the self-doubt that followed made even routine decisions feel like minefields. Weeks of declining invitations had quietly altered the rhythm of their home; they stopped cooking together. The firm noticed his withdrawal too, flagging his reduced availability during a critical structural review phase. What finally brought Vikram to the clinic was not a single breaking point but the accumulated quiet of a life narrowing to fit his own perimeter. He sat across from me now, hands folded tightly around a paper cup, and admitted that he had come because Elena had stopped sleeping on the guest bed and simply asked him to try. He was not sure what he hoped to find in this room, only that he was tired of bracing for a blow that sometimes arrived in the smell of a colleague's drink or the cadence of a hurried conversation. He feared that he would always be reacting before he could understand, that the terror would keep arriving in perfect, unblinking frames, and that he would never again feel like a man who knew which way to face the door. Still, he had come, leaving the familiar architecture of his isolation for the first time in months.
